Day 47 of 100 · Linux Administration

Cron vs systemd Timers

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityLinux AdministrationPublished journey entry

Scheduled work needs more than a time expression: execution environment, missed-run behavior, logging and dependencies determine whether a scheduler is reliable.

Architecture / mental model

schedule → cron daemon OR systemd timer → job/service → logs/result

How it works

Cron is simple and widely available for time-based commands. systemd timers integrate scheduling with service units, journal logging, dependencies and options such as persistent catch-up after a machine was offline.

The environment under a scheduler is usually smaller than an interactive shell. Scripts that only work because your personal PATH, working directory or shell profile happens to exist are fragile.

Choose based on operational needs, not fashion. A tiny independent job can be fine in cron; a service-oriented job that needs dependency management and journal visibility may fit a timer better.

Hands-on reference

crontab -l
systemctl list-timers --all
systemctl cat myjob.timer
journalctl -u myjob.service

Verification

Schedule a test execution, confirm the exact command environment and inspect its logs. For a timer using persistence, test the intended missed-run behavior in a lab.

Field note / gotcha

A job that succeeds interactively can fail under cron because PATH, current directory and environment variables are different.

Security considerations

Use dedicated service identities and protect scripts from modification by accounts that should not gain the scheduler's privileges.

What I learned

Scheduling is an execution environment, not merely a clock.
